title: Der heilige Joseph im Walde
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 201. Text from Wikisource („Der heilige Joseph im Walde (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 201 is a devotional tale rather than a fairy tale: a mother who dotes on her wicked eldest daughter and cannot bear her pious youngest keeps sending the youngest into a great forest to be rid of her, and the forest is where Saint Joseph keeps a hut. Each of the three girls in turn is given the same supper of roots to scrape and cook and offered the same single bed, and each gets in the morning exactly what her manners earned — a sack of money as heavy as she can carry, a bag a hand long, or a second nose grown fast to her own. Nothing is softened at the close: the eldest lies to her mother about a sack of gold lost on the road, and the snakes and lizards that come at the two of them there sting the child to death and the mother in the foot, for not having raised her better.

sentences.t: Es war einmal eine Mutter, die hatte drei Töchter, davon war die älteste unartig und bös, die zweite schon viel besser, obgleich sie auch ihre Fehler hatte, die jüngste aber war ein frommes gutes Kind.
sentences.l: There was once a mother, she had three daughters; of these the eldest was naughty and wicked, the second already much better, although she too had her faults, but the youngest was a pious good child.
sentences.i: There was once a mother who had three daughters. Of these the eldest was ill-natured and wicked, the second a good deal better, though she too had her faults, and the youngest was a pious, good child.
sentences.n: “die hatte drei Töchter” is the storyteller’s loose relative — ‘there was a mother, she had three daughters’ — rather than a tight subordinate clause. “davon” = of them, of these. “fromm” here means godly, devout; the whole legend turns on the word.

sentences.t: Die Mutter war aber so wunderlich, daß sie gerade die älteste Tochter am liebsten hatte und die jüngste nicht leiden konnte.
sentences.l: But the mother was so odd that she of all things had the eldest daughter dearest and could not bear the youngest.
sentences.i: But the mother was so perverse that of all three she loved the eldest daughter best and could not bear the youngest.
sentences.n: “wunderlich” = odd, contrary. “gerade” points the wrong way on purpose: of all the three, precisely that one. “am liebsten haben” = to like best; “jemanden nicht leiden können” = to be unable to stand somebody.

sentences.t: Daher schickte sie das arme Mädchen oft hinaus in einen großen Wald, um es sich vom Hals zu schaffen, denn sie dachte es würde sich verirren und nimmermehr wieder kommen.
sentences.l: Therefore she often sent the poor girl out into a great forest, to get it off her neck, for she thought it would lose its way and never come back again.
sentences.i: So she often sent the poor girl out into a great forest to be rid of her, for she thought she would lose her way and never come back.
sentences.n: “sich etwas vom Hals schaffen” = to get something off one’s neck, to be rid of it — the same figure English uses. German calls a girl das Mädchen, a neuter noun, so its pronouns are ‘it’; the literal keeps that and the idiomatic says ‘her’. “würde … verirren” is the subjunctive of reported thought.

sentences.t: Aber der Schutzengel, den jedes fromme Kind hat, verließ es nicht, sondern brachte es immer wieder auf den rechten Weg.
sentences.l: But the guardian angel that every pious child has did not forsake it, but brought it again and again onto the right way.
sentences.i: But the guardian angel that every godly child has did not forsake her, and always brought her back onto the right path.
sentences.n: The guardian angel is given as plain fact and not as a figure of speech; this is a legend rather than a fairy tale, and it states what it believes. “sondern” is the ‘but’ that follows a negative and corrects it.

sentences.t: Einmal indessen that das Schutzenglein als wenn es nicht bei der Hand wäre, und das Kind konnte sich nicht wieder aus dem Walde herausfinden.
sentences.l: Once, however, the little guardian angel did as if it were not at hand, and the child could not find its way out of the forest again.
sentences.i: One time, however, the little guardian angel acted as though it were not at hand, and the child could not find her way out of the forest.
sentences.n: “that” = tat, the 1857 spelling of tun. “als wenn … wäre” is the subjunctive of pretence: the angel only seemed to be absent. The diminutive Schutzenglein is affectionate — ‘little guardian angel’.

sentences.t: Es gieng immer fort bis es Abend wurde, da sah es in der Ferne ein Lichtchen brennen, lief darauf zu und kam vor eine kleine Hütte.
sentences.l: It kept going on until it grew evening, then it saw a little light burning in the distance, ran towards it and came before a little hut.
sentences.i: She kept walking on until evening came, and then she saw a little light burning in the distance, ran towards it and came to a little hut.
sentences.n: “immer fort” = on and on. “auf etwas zulaufen” = to run towards something, its particle split off: lief darauf zu.

sentences.t: Es klopfte an, die Thüre gieng auf, und es gelangte zu einer zweiten Thüre, wo es wieder anklopfte.
sentences.l: It knocked, the door opened, and it came to a second door, where it knocked again.
sentences.i: She knocked; the door opened, and she came to a second door, where she knocked again.
sentences.n: “Thüre” = Türe in the 1857 spelling. Three separable verbs in one line — klopfte an, gieng auf, anklopfte. The two doors are the legend’s small ceremony of approach.

sentences.t: Ein alter Mann, der einen schneeweißen Bart hatte und ehrwürdig aussah, machte ihm auf, und das war niemand anders als der heilige Joseph.
sentences.l: An old man who had a snow-white beard and looked venerable opened to it, and that was none other than Saint Joseph.
sentences.i: An old man with a snow-white beard, venerable to look at, opened to her, and that was none other than Saint Joseph.
sentences.n: “jemandem aufmachen” = to open the door to somebody, separable: machte … auf. Joseph, the husband of Mary, stands here as the poor man’s saint keeping a hut in the woods; the tale names him at once and makes no mystery of it. This is the only place the printing spells “heilige” out in full — everywhere else it abbreviates to “heil.”

sentences.t: Er sprach ganz freundlich „komm, liebes Kind, setze dich ans Feuer auf mein Stühlchen und wärme dich, ich will dir klar Wässerchen holen,
sentences.l: He said quite kindly “come, dear child, sit yourself at the fire on my little stool and warm yourself, I will fetch you clear water if you are thirsty;
sentences.i: He said very kindly, “Come, dear child, sit down by the fire on my little stool and warm yourself; I will fetch you clear water if you are thirsty;
sentences.n: “klar Wässerchen” leaves the adjective uninflected before its noun, an old form the tales keep. The diminutives pile up here — Stühlchen, Wässerchen, and the Würzelcher that follow — and they carry the poverty and the kindness at once.

sentences.t: wenn du Durst hast; zu essen aber hab ich hier im Walde nichts für dich als ein paar Würzelcher, die mußt du dir erst schaben und kochen.“
sentences.l: but to eat I have nothing here in the forest for you but a few little roots, which you must first scrape and cook for yourself.”
sentences.i: but to eat I have nothing here in the forest but a few little roots, and those you must first scrape and cook for yourself.”
sentences.n: “Würzelcher” is a dialect diminutive plural of Wurzel, ‘little roots’; the printing keeps the local form rather than the standard Würzelchen. “dir” is the dative of interest, ‘for yourself’.

sentences.t: Da reichte ihm der heil. Joseph die Wurzeln: das Mädchen schrappte sie säuberlich ab,
sentences.l: Then Saint Joseph handed it the roots: the girl scraped them clean neatly,
sentences.i: Then Saint Joseph handed her the roots, and the girl scraped them clean and carefully,
sentences.n: “heil.” is the printing’s abbreviation of heilige, ‘Saint’, and it recurs through the whole tale. “abschrappen” = to scrape off, a northern word. The youngest sister scrapes the roots clean for him; at the end of the tale the eldest will leave the dish for him to scrape.

sentences.t: dann holte es ein Stückchen Pfannkuchen, und das Brot, das ihm seine Mutter mitgegeben hatte, und that alles zusammen in einem Kesselchen beis Feuer, und kochte sich ein Mus.
sentences.l: then it fetched a little piece of pancake, and the bread that its mother had given it to take along, and put it all together in a little kettle by the fire, and cooked itself a mash.
sentences.i: then she fetched the little piece of pancake and the bread her mother had given her to take with her, put it all together in a little kettle by the fire, and cooked herself a mash.
sentences.n: “beis” = bei dem, ‘by the’ — a contraction the printing keeps from speech. “Mus” here is not jam or fruit purée but a thick cooked mash of roots and bread. “mitgeben” = to give somebody something to take along.

sentences.t: Als das fertig war, sprach der heil. Joseph „ich bin so hungrig, gib mir etwas von deinem Essen.“
sentences.l: When that was ready, Saint Joseph said “I am so hungry, give me something of your food.”
sentences.i: When it was ready, Saint Joseph said, “I am so hungry — give me some of your food.”
sentences.n: The same request comes three times, once to each sister, in almost the same words, and the three answers are the whole legend. Here the printing spells it hungrig; the two later times it has the older hungerig.

sentences.t: Da war das Kind bereitwillig und gab ihm mehr als es für sich behielt, doch war Gottes Seegen dabei, daß es satt ward.
sentences.l: Then the child was willing and gave him more than it kept for itself, yet God’s blessing was upon it, so that it grew full.
sentences.i: The child gave willingly, and gave him more than she kept for herself; yet God’s blessing was on it, so that she had her fill.
sentences.n: “Seegen” is the 1857 spelling of Segen, blessing — not a form of sehen, which the same letters can look like. “satt werden” = to become full, to eat one’s fill. The blessing is the point: giving away more leaves her with enough.

sentences.t: Als sie nun gegessen hatten, sprach der heil. Joseph „nun wollen wir zu Bett gehen:
sentences.l: When they had now eaten, Saint Joseph said “now let us go to bed:
sentences.i: When they had eaten, Saint Joseph said, “Now let us go to bed;
sentences.n: “nun wollen wir” = let us, the plain German for a proposal. “zu Bett gehen” keeps the bare noun without an article, as the old phrase does.

sentences.t: ich habe aber nur Ein Bett, lege du dich hinein, ich will mich ins Stroh auf die Erde legen.“
sentences.l: but I have only one bed, you lie down in it, I will lay myself in the straw on the ground.”
sentences.i: but I have only the one bed; you lie down in it, and I will lie in the straw on the floor.”
sentences.n: The capital in “Ein Bett” is the printing’s own way of stressing the numeral — one bed, only the one — where we would use italics. “lege du dich” puts the pronoun in after the imperative for emphasis: you take it. “sich legen” is reflexive, to lay oneself down.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete es, „bleib du nur in deinem Bett, für mich ist das Stroh weich genug.“
sentences.l: “No,” it answered, “you just stay in your bed, for me the straw is soft enough.”
sentences.i: “No,” she answered, “you stay in your bed; the straw is soft enough for me.”
sentences.n: “nur” here is the softening particle of an urging — ‘do just stay’. Each of the three sisters is offered the bed, and what she does with the offer is her whole character.

sentences.t: Der heil. Joseph aber nahm das Kind auf den Arm und trug es ins Bettchen, da that es sein Gebet und schlief ein.
sentences.l: But Saint Joseph took the child on his arm and carried it into the little bed, then it said its prayer and fell asleep.
sentences.i: But Saint Joseph took the child in his arms and carried her into the little bed, and she said her prayer and fell asleep.
sentences.n: “sein Gebet thun” = to say one’s prayer; the possessive is neuter because Kind is neuter. “einschlafen” splits: schlief … ein.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, als es aufwachte, wollte es dem heil. Joseph guten Morgen sagen, aber es sah ihn nicht.
sentences.l: The next morning, when it woke up, it wanted to say good morning to Saint Joseph, but it did not see him.
sentences.i: Next morning, when she woke, she wanted to bid Saint Joseph good morning, but she did not see him.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” = on the next morning; ander here is ‘other, next’ rather than ‘different’.

sentences.t: Da stand es auf und suchte ihn, konnte ihn aber in keiner Ecke finden:
sentences.l: Then it got up and looked for him, but could find him in no corner:
sentences.i: Then she got up and looked for him, but could not find him in any corner:
sentences.n: “aufstehen” splits: stand … auf. German negates the noun — in keiner Ecke, ‘in no corner’ — where English negates the verb.

sentences.t: endlich gewahrte es hinter der Thür einen Sack mit Geld, so schwer, als es ihn nur tragen konnte, darauf stand geschrieben das wäre für das Kind, das heute Nacht hier geschlafen hätte.
sentences.l: at last it became aware, behind the door, of a sack with money, as heavy as it could just carry, on it stood written that this was for the child that had slept here this night.
sentences.i: at last she caught sight of a sack of money behind the door, as heavy as she could carry, and on it stood written that it was for the child who had slept there that night.
sentences.n: “gewahren” = to become aware of, to catch sight of, an elevated word. “darauf stand geschrieben” is the ordinary German way of reporting an inscription — on it stood written. The two subjunctives, “wäre” and “hätte”, mark the writing as reported words.

sentences.t: Da nahm es den Sack und sprang damit fort und kam auch glücklich zu seiner Mutter, und weil es ihr alle das Geld schenkte, so konnte sie nicht anders, sie mußte mit ihm zufrieden sein.
sentences.l: Then it took the sack and sprang away with it and came safely home to its mother too, and because it gave her all the money, she could not do otherwise, she had to be satisfied with it.
sentences.i: Then she took the sack and ran off with it, and came safely home to her mother; and because she gave her all the money, the mother could do no other — she had to be satisfied with her.
sentences.n: “glücklich” here is ‘safely’, as of a journey, rather than ‘happily’. “sie konnte nicht anders” = she could do no other. The mother’s contentment is bought with the money, and the tale says so without comment.

sentences.t: Am folgenden Tag bekam das zweite Kind auch Lust in den Wald zu gehen.
sentences.l: On the following day the second child too got a desire to go into the forest.
sentences.i: The next day the second child too had a mind to go into the forest.
sentences.n: “Lust bekommen” = to take a fancy to something, to feel like doing it.

sentences.t: Die Mutter gab ihm ein viel größer Stück Pfannkuchen und Brot mit.
sentences.l: The mother gave it a much larger piece of pancake and bread to take along.
sentences.i: The mother gave her a much bigger piece of pancake and bread to take with her.
sentences.n: “größer” stands uninflected before its noun where modern German would say ein viel größeres Stück. “mitgeben” splits: gab … mit. The larger provision is this sister’s small advantage, and it does her no good.

sentences.t: Es ergieng ihm nun gerade wie dem ersten Kinde.
sentences.l: It went for it now just as for the first child.
sentences.i: Now it went with her just as it had gone with the first child.
sentences.n: “es ergeht jemandem” is impersonal — ‘it fares with somebody’ — and takes the dative: ihm, dem ersten Kinde. “Kinde” keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Abends kam es in das Hüttchen des heil. Joseph, der ihm Wurzeln zu einem Mus reichte.
sentences.l: In the evening it came into the little hut of Saint Joseph, who handed it roots for a mash.
sentences.i: In the evening she came to Saint Joseph’s little hut, and he handed her roots for a mash.
sentences.n: “Abends” is the old genitive doing duty as an adverb, ‘of an evening’. The tale now runs the same course a second time, shortened.

sentences.t: Als das fertig war, sprach er gleichfalls zu ihm „ich bin so hungerig, gib mir etwas von deinem Essen.“
sentences.l: When that was ready, he said to it likewise “I am so hungry, give me something of your food.”
sentences.i: When it was ready, he said to her likewise, “I am so hungry — give me some of your food.”
sentences.n: “hungerig” is the older form of hungrig, and the printing uses it here and in the third telling, though it had hungrig the first time. “gleichfalls” = likewise, in the same way.

sentences.t: Da antwortete das Kind „iß als mit.“
sentences.l: Then the child answered “just eat along with me.”
sentences.i: Then the child answered, “Eat along with me, then.”
sentences.n: “als” here is not the ordinary ‘as, when’ but a regional particle meaning something like ‘just, do’ — a Hessian usage the Grimms kept from the telling, and it comes again in the next speech. “mitessen” splits: iß … mit. The answer is grudging where the youngest sister’s was open-handed, and the tale lets the difference stand without comment.

sentences.t: Als ihm danach der heil. Joseph sein Bett anbot und sich aufs Stroh legen wollte, antwortete es „nein, leg dich als mit ins Bett, wir haben ja beide wohl Platz darin.“
sentences.l: When afterwards Saint Joseph offered it his bed and wanted to lie down on the straw, it answered “no, just lie down in the bed along with me, we both have room enough in it.”
sentences.i: When Saint Joseph afterwards offered her his bed and made to lie down on the straw, she answered, “No, lie down in the bed with me — there is surely room enough in it for us both.”
sentences.n: The same regional “als” again. “ja” and “wohl” are both flavouring particles, ‘after all’ and ‘surely’. This middle sister neither gives the bed up nor takes it outright, which is exactly her place between the other two.

sentences.t: Der heil. Joseph nahm es auf den Arm, legte es ins Bettchen und legte sich ins Stroh.
sentences.l: Saint Joseph took it on his arm, laid it into the little bed and lay down in the straw.
sentences.i: Saint Joseph took her in his arms, laid her in the little bed, and lay down in the straw himself.
sentences.n: The saint does what he did before, whatever the child says: the offer is his, and he keeps it.

sentences.t: Morgens, als das Kind aufwachte und den heil. Joseph suchte, war er verschwunden,
sentences.l: In the morning, when the child woke up and looked for Saint Joseph, he had vanished,
sentences.i: In the morning, when the child woke and looked for Saint Joseph, he was gone,
sentences.n: “Morgens”, like the “Abends” above, is the old genitive doing duty as an adverb.

sentences.t: aber hinter der Thüre fand es ein Säckchen mit Geld, das war händelang, und darauf stand geschrieben es wäre für das Kind, das heute Nacht hier geschlafen hätte.
sentences.l: but behind the door it found a little sack with money, that was a hand long, and on it stood written that it was for the child that had slept here this night.
sentences.i: but behind the door she found a little bag of money, a hand’s length long, and on it stood written that it was for the child who had slept there that night.
sentences.n: “händelang” = as long as a hand, and the measure is the joke: the youngest could barely lift her sack. The inscription is repeated word for word from the first night.

sentences.t: Da nahm es das Säckchen und lief damit heim, und brachte es seiner Mutter, doch behielt es heimlich ein paar Stücke für sich.
sentences.l: Then it took the little sack and ran home with it, and brought it to its mother, but secretly kept a few pieces for itself.
sentences.i: Then she took the little bag and ran home with it and brought it to her mother, but secretly kept a few coins back for herself.
sentences.n: The middle sister was called “schon viel besser” than the eldest at the start, and this is exactly how much better she is: she brings the money home and keeps a little of it. “Stücke” here are coins.

sentences.t: Nun war die älteste Tochter neugierig geworden und wollte den folgenden Morgen auch hinaus in den Wald.
sentences.l: Now the eldest daughter had grown curious and wanted the following morning to go out into the forest too.
sentences.i: Now the eldest daughter had grown curious, and the next morning she too wanted to go out into the forest.
sentences.n: The verb of motion is left out after “wollte” — wanted out into the forest — which German does freely with a modal. “den folgenden Morgen” is the accusative of time.

sentences.t: Die Mutter gab ihr Pfannkuchen mit, so viel sie wollte, Brot und auch Käse dazu.
sentences.l: The mother gave her pancake to take along, as much as she wanted, bread and cheese besides.
sentences.i: The mother gave her pancakes to take with her, as much as she wanted, and bread and cheese besides.
sentences.n: Note the pronoun: “ihr”, ‘her’, where the two younger sisters were “ihm”, ‘it’. Here the tale calls her die Tochter, a feminine noun; a sentence or two later it goes back to “es” for das Mädchen and das Kind.

sentences.t: Abends fand sie den heil. Joseph in seinem Hüttchen gerade so, wie ihn die zwei andern gefunden hatten.
sentences.l: In the evening she found Saint Joseph in his little hut just as the two others had found him.
sentences.i: In the evening she found Saint Joseph in his little hut exactly as the two others had found him.
sentences.n: “gerade so, wie” = just as. By now the tale is telling itself in the reader’s memory, and it marks only the differences.

sentences.t: Als das Mus fertig war und der heil. Joseph sprach „ich bin so hungerig, gib mir etwas von deinem Essen,“
sentences.l: When the mash was ready and Saint Joseph said “I am so hungry, give me something of your food,”
sentences.i: When the mash was ready and Saint Joseph said, “I am so hungry — give me some of your food,”
sentences.n: The third and last time the request comes, in the same words as before.

sentences.t: antwortete das Mädchen „warte, bis ich satt bin, was ich dann überig lasse, das sollst du haben.“
sentences.l: the girl answered “wait until I am full; what I then leave over, that you shall have.”
sentences.i: the girl answered, “Wait until I have had my fill; what I leave over then, you shall have.”
sentences.n: “überig” is the 1857 spelling of übrig, left over. The resumptive “das” picks the whole first clause up again before the main verb, a German habit English has no need of.

sentences.t: Es aß aber beinah alles auf und der heil. Joseph mußte das Schüsselchen ausschrappen.
sentences.l: But it ate up nearly everything and Saint Joseph had to scrape out the little dish.
sentences.i: But she ate up nearly all of it, and Saint Joseph had to scrape out the little dish.
sentences.n: “aufessen” splits: aß … auf. The saint scraping the empty dish answers the youngest sister scraping the roots clean for him — the legend makes its point by symmetry rather than by saying it.

sentences.t: Der gute Alte bot ihm hernach sein Bett an und wollte auf dem Stroh liegen,
sentences.l: The good old man afterwards offered it his bed and wanted to lie on the straw,
sentences.i: The good old man afterwards offered her his bed and meant to lie on the straw,
sentences.n: “hernach” = afterwards. He is called “der gute Alte”, the good old man, just as she is about to take everything he has.

sentences.t: das nahm es ohne Widerrede an, legte sich in das Bettchen und ließ dem Greis das harte Stroh.
sentences.l: that it accepted without a word of objection, laid itself in the little bed and left the old man the hard straw.
sentences.i: she accepted it without a word, lay down in the little bed and left the old man the hard straw.
sentences.n: “annehmen” splits, and its object “das” is thrown to the front of the sentence: das nahm es an. “ohne Widerrede” = without demur. “Greis” is the word for a very old man, and it is chosen here to make the taking worse.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen, wie es aufwachte, war der heil. Joseph nicht zu finden, doch darüber machte es sich keine Sorgen: es suchte hinter der Thüre nach einem Geldsack.
sentences.l: The next morning, as it woke up, Saint Joseph was not to be found, but about that it made itself no worries: it looked behind the door for a money-sack.
sentences.i: Next morning, when she woke, Saint Joseph was nowhere to be found, but she gave herself no concern about that: she looked behind the door for a money bag.
sentences.n: “nicht zu finden” = not to be found, an infinitive with passive force. “sich Sorgen machen” = to worry. She has come for the sack, and the tale lets that be seen.

sentences.t: Es kam ihm vor als läge etwas auf der Erde, doch weil es nicht recht unterscheiden konnte, was es war, bückte es sich und stieß mit seiner Nase daran.
sentences.l: It seemed to it as if something were lying on the ground, but because it could not rightly make out what it was, it bent down and knocked against it with its nose.
sentences.i: It seemed to her that something was lying on the floor; but because she could not rightly make out what it was, she bent down and knocked against it with her nose.
sentences.n: “es kommt jemandem vor” = it seems to somebody, impersonal and with the dative. “läge” is the subjunctive of what only seemed to be. What the thing on the ground is, the tale never says, then or afterwards.

sentences.t: Aber es blieb an der Nase hangen, und wie es sich aufrichtete, sah es zu seinem Schrecken, daß es noch eine zweite Nase war, die an der seinen festhieng.
sentences.l: But it stayed hanging on the nose, and as it raised itself up, it saw to its horror that it was a second nose, which hung fast to its own.
sentences.i: But it stuck fast to her nose, and as she straightened up she saw to her horror that it was a second nose, hanging fast to her own.
sentences.n: “hangen” is the older form of hängen, and “festhieng” is festhing, with the same ie spelling as gieng and fieng. The punishment is grotesque rather than deadly, and it is meant to be laughed at.

sentences.t: Da hub es an zu schreien und zu heulen, aber das half nichts, es mußte immer auf seine Nase sehen, wie die so weit hinausstand.
sentences.l: Then it began to scream and to howl, but that helped nothing, it had to keep looking at its nose, how it stood out so far.
sentences.i: Then she began to scream and howl, but that was no help; she could not stop looking at her nose, and how far it stood out.
sentences.n: “hub … an” is the old past of anheben, ‘began’, a fixed storyteller’s turn. “das half nichts” = that was no use. The last clause hangs on “sehen” as a wie-clause: saw how far it stood out.

sentences.t: Da lief es in einem Geschrei fort, bis es dem heil. Joseph begegnete,
sentences.l: Then it ran away in one long screaming, until it met Saint Joseph,
sentences.i: Then she ran off in one long scream until she met Saint Joseph,
sentences.n: “in einem Geschrei” = in one continuous outcry. “begegnen” takes the dative: dem heil. Joseph begegnen, to meet him.

sentences.t: dem fiel es zu Füßen und bat so lange, bis er aus Mitleid ihm die Nase wieder abnahm und noch zwei Pfennige schenkte.
sentences.l: at whose feet it fell, and begged so long until out of pity he took the nose off it again and gave it two pennies besides.
sentences.i: and she fell at his feet and begged so long that out of pity he took the nose off her again, and gave her two pennies besides.
sentences.n: “dem” opens the clause as a relative, ‘to whom’, picking up Joseph; “zu Füßen fallen” takes the dative. The two pennies close the account: she came for a sackful and leaves with two coins.

sentences.t: Als es daheim ankam, stand vor der Thüre seine Mutter und fragte „was hast du geschenkt kriegt?“
sentences.l: When it arrived at home, its mother stood before the door and asked “what have you got given?”
sentences.i: When she got home, her mother was standing at the door and asked, “What were you given?”
sentences.n: “geschenkt kriegt” is the colloquial passive of everyday speech — kriegen, to get, with a past participle, and the participle of kriegen itself left without its ge-. The mother asks about the present before she looks at her daughter’s face.

sentences.t: Da log es und antwortete „einen großen Sack voll Gelds, aber ich habe ihn unterwegs verloren.“
sentences.l: Then it lied and answered “a great sack full of money, but I have lost it on the way.”
sentences.i: Then she lied and answered, “A great sack full of money — but I lost it on the way.”
sentences.n: “voll Gelds” takes the old genitive after voll, full of money. “log” is the past of lügen, to lie.

sentences.t: „Verloren!“ rief die Mutter, „o den wollen wir schon wieder finden,“ nahm es bei der Hand und wollte mit ihm suchen.
sentences.l: “Lost!” cried the mother, “oh, we shall find it again all right,” took it by the hand and wanted to go looking with it.
sentences.i: “Lost!” cried the mother. “Oh, we shall find it again soon enough” — and she took her by the hand and set off to look with her.
sentences.n: “schon” here is the particle of confidence, ‘right enough, never fear’. The sentence changes its subject without saying so: the mother cries out, then takes, then wants.

sentences.t: Zuerst fieng es an zu weinen und wollte nicht mit gehen, endlich aber gieng es mit,
sentences.l: At first it began to cry and would not go along, but at last it went along,
sentences.i: At first she began to cry and would not go, but at last she went along,
sentences.n: “fieng … an” is fing an, began, in the 1857 spelling. “mitgehen” is printed apart here as mit gehen and joined a clause later as gieng es mit.

sentences.t: doch auf dem Wege kamen so viele Eidechsen und Schlangen auf sie beide los, daß sie sich nicht zu retten wußten;
sentences.l: but on the way so many lizards and snakes came at the two of them that they did not know how to save themselves;
sentences.n: “auf jemanden los kommen” = to come at somebody, to make for them, with los at the end. “sich nicht zu retten wissen” = not to know how to save oneself.

sentences.t: sie stachen auch endlich das böse Kind todt, und die Mutter stachen sie in den Fuß, weil sie es nicht besser erzogen hatte.
sentences.l: and at last they stung the wicked child dead, and the mother they stung in the foot, because she had not brought it up better.
sentences.i: and at last they stung the wicked child to death; and the mother they stung in the foot, because she had not brought her up better.
sentences.n: “todt stechen” = to sting or stab to death, the particle at the end. The legend kills the eldest daughter outright and punishes the mother for the upbringing, and it offers this as justice with no softening and no apology. The last clause simply gives the reason: sie hatte es nicht besser erzogen.

glossary.als: als — as, when; than (after a comparative); in this tale also a regional particle of urging, roughly ‘just, do’ (iß als mit = iß nur mit, just eat along) — a Hessian usage
glossary.alter: alt — old (masc. nom. sg.: ein alter Mann, an old man)
glossary.daher: daher — therefore, for that reason (Daher schickte sie das arme Mädchen hinaus); also daher — along, this way (kam daher, came along)
glossary.gerade: gerade — just, exactly, precisely (gerade so, wie … = just as …)
glossary.heil: heilig — holy, saint (here always the abbreviation ‘heil.’ = heilige, as in der heil. Joseph, Saint Joseph)
glossary.lasse: lassen — to leave, leave over (1st sg. present: was ich überig lasse, what I leave over); also to let, to allow
glossary.leg: legen — lay, put (imperative sg.); sich legen = to lie down (leg dich ins Bett, lie down in the bed)
glossary.mus: das Mus — mush, a thick cooked mash (here of roots, bread and pancake)
glossary.schaffen: schaffen — to get, to bring about (sich etwas vom Hals schaffen, to get something off one’s neck, to be rid of it); also to provide, to manage
glossary.seegen: der Seegen — blessing (1857 spelling of Segen; not a form of sehen)
glossary.setze: sich setzen — sit down, seat oneself (imperative sg.: setze dich ans Feuer, sit down by the fire)
glossary.stachen: stechen — stung, stabbed (3rd pl. past; here of lizards and snakes; todt stechen, to sting to death)
